events.title: Prof. Dr. Marina Tropmann-Frick
events.summary: Rethinking AI: From Perceived Intelligence to Measurable Responsibility
events.speaker: Prof. Marina Tropmann-Frick
events.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is shifting from a collection of tools to an epistemic computational method that reshapes how knowledge is generated, evaluated and applied. This talk presents recent advances in generative and reasoning models, highlighting both their capabilities and the limitations of current evaluation practices. Building on this, the talk introduces AI as a medium, emphasizing its role in transforming research workflows and education through hybrid human-AI reasoning and AI-augmented knowledge production. This shift challenges established methodological assumptions and requires new evaluation paradigms. Finally, the talk situates these developments within Responsible AI, arguing that performance metrics alone are insufficient. Using metrics-based assessment across fairness, robustness, privacy, and explainability, it demonstrates the need for systematic evaluation frameworks to ensure trustworthy deployment.
events.affiliation: Hamburg University of Applied Sciences (HAW Hamburg)

events.title: Dr. Xiaoping Wang
events.summary: From Beamtime to Publication: Trustworthy AI to Accelerate Neutron Diffraction Workflows
events.speaker: Dr. Xiaoping Wang
events.abstract: DOE user facilities are entering a phase where the central challenge is not only collecting data, but also converting data into validated scientific outcomes at scale. A step-change in scientific throughput will come from workflows that shorten the beamtime-to-publication path while strengthening reproducibility across instruments, teams, and proposal cycles. In that context, we are developing two complementary AI-enabled capabilities for single-crystal neutron diffraction at the Spallation Neutron Source: CrystalPilot, to support experiment planning and live decision-making, and NeuDiff Agent, to accelerate analysis and reporting with reproducibility built in. This presentation focuses on NeuDiff Agent, where the near-term impact on user productivity and facility throughput is most direct. At neutron user facilities, the beamtime-to-publication gap is increasingly a practical rate-limiting step. For single-crystal time-of-flight neutron diffraction, small differences in reduction settings and refinement choices can cascade into different outcomes, extra rework, and avoidable validation problems at submission. These effects are most apparent for hydrogen-rich samples, subtle disorder, and weak symmetry breaking, where the analysis is particularly sensitive to workflow choices. NeuDiff Agent is an AI-assisted workflow developed for the TOPAZ diffractometer that helps move a dataset from instrument outputs to a submission-quality structure CIF, while retaining a clear record of the key processing steps and decisions. The system separates scientific intent from configuration entry, checks settings for internal consistency, generates analysis inputs, runs established reduction and refinement tools, and returns structured guidance aimed at common CIF validation issues before submission. In an end-to-end representative case, NeuDiff Agent delivered a greater than four-fold reduction in time from neutron event data to a submission-quality structure CIF, while producing an output with no checkCIF level A or B alerts. The key takeaway is straightforward: speed only matters if it is dependable in real scientific workflows. We will share what we learned about reliability, failure modes, and evaluation, and show how a trustworthy AI-assisted workflow can improve facility efficiency, reduce analyst burden, and make neutron diffraction results easier to validate, reproduce, and publish.

events.title: Prof. Dr. Stephan Roth
events.summary: Retrieving cluster growth using deep-learning using in situ sputter deposition and GISAXS
events.speaker: Prof. Dr. Stephan Volkher Roth
events.abstract: Extracting morphological parameters from supported cluster layers allows for predicting their optoelectronic properties, which are important for electronics or sensors. Here, in situ grazing incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS) is a powerful technique to analyze quantitatively the growth, connectivity, and changing morphology of these cluster layers during sputter deposition. However, the interpretation of GISAXS pattern necessitates the use of simulation- and model-based analysis routines. The GISAXS pattern are calculated based on real-space structures, taking into account the reflection and refraction effects during the scattering process. We extract morphological parameters, such as the cluster radius, the average inter-cluster distance and their distributions when using artificial neural networks trained on simulated GISAXS pattern. We are able to estimate the entire distribution of morphological parameters and directly compare it to a phenomenological growth model, using the well-known gold-on-silicon bilayer system as reference. In detail, we are for the first time able to distinguish temperature-dependent nucleation and growth processes which occur concurrently during the whole sputter deposition process. Finally, we will address the current limitations and solutions incorporating a small portion of complementary data into the training.
events.affiliation: DESY and KTH Royal Institute of Technology

events.title: Dr. Daniel Pajerowski
events.summary: MAIQMag: Multimodal AI for 2D Quantum Magnets
events.speaker: Dr. Daniel Pajerowski
events.abstract: Determining the microscopic Hamiltonian of a quantum magnet is a central challenge in condensed matter physics. Modern materials often exhibit competing interactions, anisotropies, and emergent behavior that cannot be uniquely constrained by any single measurement. Neutron scattering, x-ray spectroscopies, and bulk probes each provide important but incomplete views of the underlying physics, making Hamiltonian inference a difficult multimodal inverse problem. In this talk, I will present the vision and early progress of MAIQMag (Multimodal AI for Hamiltonian Inference in Quantum Magnets), a physics-informed machine learning effort to infer uncertainty-aware magnetic Hamiltonians from heterogeneous experimental data. Rather than treating each dataset in isolation, MAIQMag aims to combine forward models for neutron spectroscopy, diffraction, x-ray measurements, and thermodynamic observables with AI methods that learn jointly across modalities. This approach is designed to identify which measurements most strongly constrain exchange interactions, anisotropies, and effective spin degrees of freedom, while also quantifying uncertainty and model ambiguity. MAIQMag is organized around four connected thrusts. First, we are building AI-ready multimodal data pipelines that connect neutron, x-ray, and bulk measurements through shared formats, metadata, and analysis pathways. Second, we are advancing physics-based forward models for scattering and thermodynamic observables to generate realistic synthetic training data and enable fast surrogate-assisted inference. Third, we are benchmarking machine-learning approaches against conventional analysis and controlled case studies to identify where multimodal AI provides real gains in accuracy, efficiency, and uncertainty quantification. Fourth, we are demonstrating end-to-end workflows on representative quantum magnets to establish portable analysis strategies that can scale across instruments and facilities. More broadly, MAIQMag highlights an emerging role for machine learning in scattering science: not as a replacement for physics, but as a framework for integrating complementary measurements into interpretable, predictive models of complex materials.

events.title: Prof. Dr. Peter Müller-Buschbaum
events.summary: Structure Formation in Functional Films Revealed by Machine-Learning-Supported Grazing-Incidence Small-Angle X-ray Scattering
events.speaker: Prof. Dr. Peter Müller-Buschbaum
events.abstract: Grazing-incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS) is a powerful tool for studying the structure formation of functional films and relating it to the properties and performances of novel materials. With the high brilliance of synchrotron sources, in situ studies reveal the formation kinetics of these functional films on the millisecond scale for deposition methods such as spin-coating, spraying, printing, and sputter deposition. However, especially with the large amount of data generated over very short time scales during an in situ GISAXS experiment following the film formation, successful data analysis becomes increasingly time-consuming and laborious, requiring long-term experience on the part of the experimenter. To overcome this challenge and accelerate the analysis of time-resolved GISAXS data, we use machine learning with neural networks. Using synthetic data generated by simulations and experimental data from time-resolved in situ GISAXS experiments, the network is trained to analyze 2D GISAXS patterns. As a result, the neural network trained on synthetic GISAXS data directly predicts domain-size distributions from experimental two-dimensional scattering patterns, capturing the full kinetics of nanostructure evolution with high temporal resolution. The predictions reveal hierarchical size distributions and periodic growth features, consistent with previous findings and validated by complementary scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging. The goal of this approach is to enable on-the-fly analysis simultaneous with measurement at the synchrotron, thereby opening GISAXS to a broader scientific community that benefits from the method but lacks the capacity to analyze the complex GISAXS data.

events.title: Dr. Chi-Huan Tung
events.summary: Correlation as a Robust and Efficient Organizing Principle for Count-Limited Multipixel Measurements
events.speaker: Dr. Chi-Huan Tung
events.abstract: Scattering measurements are fundamentally limited by Poisson counting statistics, which often require extended acquisition times to achieve the desired level of precision. This work develops a Bayesian inference framework that improves effective measurement quality by explicitly exploiting correlations among neighboring data points during analysis. Rather than treating individual measurements as statistically independent, the method represents the underlying scattering intensity as a correlated field within a Gaussian-process formulation. By incorporating these correlations, reliable estimates can be obtained from substantially fewer detected counts, providing a practical route to accelerate neutron and X-ray scattering experiments. The study also presents a first-principle analysis of the statistical limits associated with binning and smoothing. Explicit expressions for the mean-squared error are derived as functions of bin width and smoothing scale, revealing a quantitative trade-off between spatial resolution and statistical uncertainty. This analysis also clarifies the conditions under which such approaches outperform conventional histogram representations. The resulting optimality conditions offer practical guidance for selecting binning and smoothing parameters and demonstrate that correlation-aware inference can improve statistical efficiency without requiring hardware modifications.

events.title: Dr. Marshall T. McDonnell
events.summary: Commissioning on-the-fly, Autonomous Neutron Scattering Experiments using an Interconnected Science Ecosystem Approach
events.speaker: Dr. Marshall T. McDonnell
events.abstract: Recent work for commissioning autonomous neutron scattering experiments performed at the Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) and High Flux Isotope Reactor (HFIR) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) will be presented. These experiments mark progress for beamlines to prepare for more automation and steering in both x-ray and neutron scattering. Emphasis will be on creating a shared, interconnected ecosystem of scattering instruments and compute capabilities. This approach has been used to perform autonomous neutron scattering experiments on the VULCAN, NOMAD, POWGEN, and BioSANS beamlines, spanning engineering diffraction, powder diffraction, and small-angle scattering techniques. These experiments helped bring together multiple software infrastructures including External Instrument Control, Interconnected Science Ecosystem (INTERSECT), Distributed INTERSECT Active Learning for Experiment Design (DIALED), and National Science Data Fabric. Together, this infrastructure enabled analysis to run on compute resources from outside the beamline network and stream data outside ORNL to the National Science Data Fabric. Future experiments are already planned to extend this same interconnected ecosystem approach to x-ray scattering at the Cornell High-Energy Synchrotron Source.

events.title: Dr. Jan Ilavsky
events.summary: USAXS Detector-to-Paper Data Pipeline for Scattering Data in the Age of Al
events.speaker: Dr. Jan Ilavsky
events.abstract: Artificial Intelligence promises a revolutionary increase in productivity and scientific discovery in science, though its exact impact remains unclear. Synchrotron small-angle and wide-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS/WAXS) techniques are particularly promising for Al applications because they are well-established, with mature applications, data reduction, and analysis pipelines. These techniques have been successfully applied across diverse fields, for example, in the structural optimization of next-generation materials. Consequently, Al implementation should be theoretically straightforward, especially in focused domains such as polymer science and metallurgy. The combination of rapid data collection and swift Al analysis enables self-directed, automated experiments. Key prerequisites for such experiments are robust data pipelines that quickly and automatically process data after collection-including complete normalization, background subtraction, reduction, calibration, and, critically, meaningful analysis to generate quantitative materials parameters that Al models can use for experiment guidance. An additional, even more challenging step is including sufficient materials metadata with each sample. While our instrument has provided the capability for 10+ years to include extensive materials parameters with each sample, and the HDF5 format is uniquely suitable for extensive metadata inclusion, our experience shows that practically no one includes such information-especially for samples where data collection times are shorter than the time required for manual metadata entry. This challenge can be addressed through automated experiments; assuming machine-readable logbooks from sample preparation, Al could potentially assist. This talk reviews the current status of data handling at the USAXS-SAXS-WAXS instrument at the Advanced Photon Source, which provides a fully automatic data reduction pipeline yielding combined HDF5 files in NXsas and NXcanSAS formats. These data have been successfully used by users of the AFL instrument. The upcoming implementation of automatic model fitting will be discussed and existing code demonstrated.

events.title: Dr. Zhongcan Xiao
events.summary: CrystalPilot: AI-accelerated single-crystal neutron diffraction at the Spallation Neutron Source
events.speaker: Dr. Zhongcan Xiao
events.abstract: Neutron single-crystal diffraction at large user facilities is often limited by experiment overhead and delayed feedback during beamtime, which can reduce data quality and efficiency. We develop CrystalPilot, an integrated experiment platform that unifies monitoring, steering, and on-the-fly analysis for single-crystal neutron diffraction at the Spallation Neutron Source, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL). Built on the NOVA-Trame framework with an MVVM architecture and deployed through ORNL’s Neutron Data Interpretation Platform (NDIP), CrystalPilot provides a scalable pathway to stream live data to high-performance computing resources and return actionable guidance while measurements are in progress. The platform delivers live estimates of data quality and completeness from counting statistics and uses crystallographic symmetry to recommend efficient orientation and acquisition strategies. For data fidelity, CrystalPilot applies AI-assisted background estimation and artifact suppression to improve integration robustness and downstream refinement stability. A central design goal is to make facility workflows more reproducible and auditable by standardizing configurations, capturing decision context, and enabling consistent execution across instruments, teams, and proposal cycles. Ongoing development focuses on integrating an agentic layer that automates routine steps while retaining explicit user authorization at critical checkpoints, supporting trustworthy acceleration from beamtime to validated structural results at scale. This directly supports governed, near-real-time decision-making required for next-generation, highly efficient user operations.

events.title: Dr. Viktor Reshniak
events.summary: Physics-Constrained Peak Integration in Time-of-Flight Neutron Scattering
events.speaker: Dr. Viktor Reshniak
events.abstract: Recent advances in unsupervised learning have enabled data-driven analysis of time-of-flight (TOF) neutron scattering data with minimal reliance on manual intervention. In earlier work, we introduced a scale-space framework for robust characterization of Bragg features directly from raw data. Here, we build on that foundation and develop a physics-informed approach to peak shape estimation and integration that explicitly incorporates the global wavelength dependence of Bragg peak widths. Rather than fitting each reflection independently, the method enforces a shared, physically motivated model that links peak shapes across the full dataset. This global constraint yields a coherent description of peak broadening as a function of wavelength, enabling more stable and consistent integration, particularly for weak, noisy, or partially overlapping reflections. By combining data-driven representation with physically constrained modeling, the proposed framework improves the reliability of extracted intensities while retaining flexibility across varying experimental conditions. Applications to challenging TOF datasets demonstrate that enforcing global wavelength-dependent behavior leads to gains in robustness and integration accuracy compared to conventional local fitting approaches.

events.title: Prof. Kamal Choudhary
events.summary: AGAPI-XRD: Hybrid DiffractGPT-Rietveld Refinement Framework for Automated X-ray Diffraction Analysis
events.speaker: Prof. Kamal Choudhary
events.abstract: X-ray diffraction (XRD) remains one of the most powerful experimental techniques for characterizing materials, yet the path from raw diffraction data to a refined atomic structure continues to demand significant domain expertise and manual intervention. We present AGAPI-XRD, a hybrid computational framework that integrates DiffractGPT, a generative pretrained transformer trained on thousands of crystal structures and their simulated XRD patterns with classical Rietveld refinement into a unified, accessible API hosted on the AtomGPT.org API (AGAPI) platform. DiffractGPT can rapidly predict candidate atomic structures from experimental XRD patterns. These AI-generated structures then serve as high-quality starting configurations for automated Rietveld refinement, dramatically reducing sensitivity to initial guess quality and accelerating convergence. We benchmark our approach across diverse crystal systems in the RRUFF database. By bridging generative AI with established crystallographic refinement, AGAPI-XRD lowers the barrier to automated structure determination and advances the vision of fully autonomous materials characterization pipelines. The combined pipeline is exposed through the AGAPI interface at https://atomgpt.org/xrd.

events.title: Dr. Aileen Luo
events.summary: PtychoFM: Toward a Foundation Model for Ptychographic Imaging
events.speaker: Dr. Aileen Luo
events.abstract: Ptychography is a scanning coherent diffractive imaging technique that uniquely enables simultaneous recovery of a complex-valued object and probe from a series of overlapping diffraction patterns, with applications spanning X-ray, electron, and optical imaging. Real-time reconstruction remains a fundamental bottleneck: conventional iterative solvers require hundreds to thousands of iterations per dataset and are sensitive to initialization, while supervised machine learning approaches do not generalize well to different experimental conditions. We have developed PtychoFM, a physics-aware vision transformer-based neural network that directly embeds a differentiable ptychographic forward model into its architecture; the model learns to reconstruct the object magnitude and phase by minimizing the discrepancy between its physics-simulated and measured diffraction intensities. We demonstrated PtychoFM at the APS/CNM hard X-ray nanoprobe on an integrated circuit sample measured at 200 Hz and reconstructed at 7 nm pixel size, supporting real-time deployment on relevant samples at the instrument with competitive resolution. Pre-trained and fine-tuned PtychoFM lowers the barrier to expert-quality reconstruction across different probes and experimental conditions.

events.title: Dr. Bowen Zheng
events.summary: Machine Learning–Augmented Acceleration of Iterative Ptychographic Reconstruction
events.speaker: Dr. Bowen Zheng
events.abstract: Iterative ptychographic reconstruction algorithms are widely used for coherent diffractive imaging but can exhibit slow convergence under realistic experimental conditions. We propose a machine learning–augmented approach that accelerates iterative ptychographic reconstruction by introducing a learned fast-forward operator applied during reconstruction. Following an initial warm-up using standard iterations, the fast-forward operator advances the reconstruction toward a more converged state, after which conventional iterative updates are resumed. This strategy preserves the physical consistency and flexibility of established ptychographic solvers while reducing the number of iterations required for convergence. The model is trained on diverse ptychographic datasets and evaluated on experimental data acquired in a different year, demonstrating robustness and temporal generalization. Compared with conventional iterative solvers, the machine learning-augmented method achieves comparable reconstruction quality while converging faster in terms of Poisson negative log-likelihood, corresponding to a more than two-fold reduction in wall-clock time. The approach has been integrated into an existing reconstruction pipeline and deployed in production at a synchrotron beamline, demonstrating practicality for real-time experimental operation.
events.affiliation: Advanced Light Source, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory

events.title: Prof. Boran Ma
events.summary: Toward Chemistry-Aware Machine Learning Models for Polymeric Materials Design
events.speaker: Prof. Boran Ma
events.abstract: Machine learning (ML) has played a critical role in enhancing the understanding of the fundamental relationships in the materials science paradigm, as well as accelerating design optimizations when combined with high throughput experimentation. Efficiently extracting meaningful physicochemical information from the representations of polymeric materials remains a challenge in ML for polymeric material systems. This presentation will showcase our work on developing ML models for the predictive control of polymeric materials morphology. Strategic manipulation of physicochemical features of structural representation as well as design and fine-tuning of model architecture will be discussed. Featurization and model architecture design strategies will be highlighted, leading toward the development of chemistry-aware ML models for polymeric material systems. This chemistry-aware ML model framework, integrated with high throughput experimentation with grazing-incidence small-angle x-ray scattering, allows for rapid data analysis and explainable composition–processing–property relationship prediction, establishing the foundation for exploring the vast design space of polymeric materials for various applications.

events.title: Dr. Haili Jia
events.summary: Revealing local structure and defects through multimodal spectroscopy and machine learning
events.speaker: Dr. Haili Jia
events.abstract: Modern materials characterization is generating richer and faster data than ever before, but a central challenge remains: how do we convert complex measurements into reliable knowledge of local structure and defects? This challenge is especially acute in three-dimensional materials, where the signature of a single point defect is often diluted by surrounding atoms, finite probe volumes, and overlapping spectral features, making it difficult to detect directly from any single measurement. In this talk, I will present our recent multimodal framework that connects spectroscopy, simulation, and machine learning to improve local structure and defect inference from complex data. As a case study, I will discuss our recent work on lithium nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) cathodes using X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS), ab initio spectral simulations, and machine learning. By combining O K-edge and transition-metal L-edge information across multiple elements and modalities, this approach uses complementary spectral sensitivity to resolve local chemistry more effectively than single-stream analysis alone. Within this framework, we infer local element content, identify local coordination environments, and detect signatures associated with oxygen vacancies and antisite disorder. The model is validated by experimental data, supports spatially resolved defect analysis, and remains physically interpretable by linking the most informative spectral regions back to local atomic and electronic structure. Multimodal learning also improves robustness to noise and outperforms unimodal inputs across multiple local structure and defect inference tasks. More broadly, I will use this example to discuss multimodal spectroscopy as a step toward an inference layer for materials characterization: a quantitative bridge between measurement and structure that helps extract otherwise inaccessible information in complex materials systems, including defect-rich and spatially heterogeneous materials.
